title: Vega: how implied volatility moves your option price
summary: Vega is an option's price sensitivity to implied volatility, in dollars per one point of IV. It is highest near the money and larger for longer-dated options. Vega does not matter at expiration, but it sets the entry price. Put on long-vega trades when IV is low and short-vega trades when IV is high. You can be right on direction and still lose to vega.

steps.caption: A $100 stock and a one-year at-the-money call.
Vega peaks near the money: the dollar change per one point of IV.
Move the strike away from the price: vega falls.
Cut days to expiry from 365 to 7: vega shrinks. Long-dated options carry far more vega.
Delta shows direction. A good directional call can still lose if IV falls.
Theta is the daily cost of holding the long option.

takeaways: Vega is the option price change per one point of implied volatility.
Vega is highest near the money and larger for long-dated options.
Buy vega when IV is low; sell vega when IV is high.
Second-order Greeks such as vanna and volga matter less than vega for most traders.
